title: The Core
full_review:
A manned spaceship must penetrate deep into Earth to restabilize its core or the world will end in the heady sci-fi thriller "The Core" (Paramount).

With lavish production design, sharp ensemble cast and wealth of special effects, director Jon Amiel crafts a fairly suspenseful film. But at 136 minutes it's overlong, some dialogue falls flat, and, most of all, it's pretty preposterous. Yet it does provide disaster-movie entertainment with some eye-popping visuals.

The intriguing opening has scientists Dr. Josh Keyes (Aaron Eckhart) and Dr. Levesque (Tcheky Karyo) guessing that the sudden deaths of 32 Bostonians was due to the electromagnetic failure of their pacemakers. But they realize there may be global implications when flocks of pigeons lose their way over London, crashing into windows and pedestrians in a scene instantly reminiscent of Hitchcock's "The Birds."

Josh becomes convinced the planet is doomed by an electromagnetic failure in Earth's core after a spaceship loses its bearings over Los Angeles -- and only the quick thinking of Maj. Beck Childs (Hilary Swank) and skill of Cmdr. Iverson (Bruce Greenwood) enable the ship to land safely without crashing into Dodger Stadium.

The government quickly enlists these scientists and astronauts and pre-eminent geophysicist Dr. Zimsky (Stanley Tucci) to penetrate the core and reset its electromagnetic rotation. But to get there they need the brilliantly eccentric Dr. Brazzleton (Delroy Lindo), whose invention of a subterranean craft can pierce the earth without crushing from the exterior pressure. The urgency increases when erratic lightning intensifies over Rome, imploding its ancient monuments.

It's visually engaging as the six burrow into the planet. But a repetitive structure sets in: a problem, deadly danger, hopelessness, then sudden inspiration that saves the mission until the next round of obstacles. It gets far-fetched in the extreme when the craft is stuck among giant crystals and several venture outside to free it, claiming their spacesuits can withstand the pressure.

One by one the crew's numbers diminish as at different stages the ultimate sacrifice is called for to keep the mission on target. Well-acted characterizations and exceptional production values keep the overlong story moving along as the film avoids becoming too solemn or slipping into a campy mode.

Tucci seems to relish his role as the supreme egotist who gets to throw a hissy fit before bringing his deliciously arrogant character full circle. Eckhart and Swank keep the emotions grounded with only the slightest hint of potential romance if they ever resurface. Back at Mission Control, D.J. Qualls brings a sense of mischief to his role as a computer hacker hired by the government to keep the secret project off the Web lest mass panic ensue. Scientific mumbo-jumbo explanations are kept to a minimum, and it ends on an upbeat note despite a disaster in San Francisco bound to chill moviegoers in these anxious times.

Due to scenes of mayhem, lethal danger and an instance of rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
